newsitem.title: USA: US antitrust regulator moves away from quick fixes.
newsitem.headline: US antitrust regulator moves away from quick fixes.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission's top merger litigator said Friday the commission is moving away from accepting quick fixes, choosing instead to challenge flawed deals and permit others to go through.

"We're not in the horsetrading business, we are not in the business of compromise because 'something is better than nothing,' if we don't really believe it solves the problem," said George Cary in an interview.
Cary was speaking generally, and not about specific actions of the FTC, such as the FTC's rejection Friday of a merger between Staples Inc. and Office Depot.
Rather, his comments were directed at what he sees as a gradual trend by the FTC. In fact, the Staples case is only the latest of many transactions in which the FTC has moved toward the new approach.
As Cary and others see it, the tendency of the FTC now is to require huge changes in flawed transactions or to reject them entirely.

This has coincided with new theories of competition to match changes in the economy. For example, a year ago, the FTC rejected the proposed merger of pharmacy chains Rite Aid and Revco, even though the merger would have preserved competition at the retail level.

Instead, the FTC focused on contracts between the emerging number of national health-care providers and large regional pharmacy chains. They reasoned that competition must be preserved between the chains of pharmacies that could negotiate such big contracts. trend," he said.
Steve Sunshine of Shearman and Sterling in Washington said he expected to see both the FTC and the antitrust division of the Justice Department become more aggressive.
He believes the tougher stance has come about because government lawyers have reviewed their cases and found past compromise agreements have in some cases been ineffective.
Staples and Office Depot had agreed to sell 63 stores from a total of more than 1,000 but the FTC said that even with the divestiture, prices would have increased to consumers.
"They had a pretty good settlement on the table in the Staples case," Sunshine said. "They could have taken it with a fair amount of face."
